lead.headline: Athletics idle by law on Sunday, one victory short of the pennant
lead.deck: Pennsylvania's Sabbath statute keeps Shibe Park shut; Chicago to play there this afternoon; Yankees and Brooklyn divide; Giants win at the Polo Grounds before about 31,000
lead.body: The Philadelphia Athletics, needing one victory to be certain of the American League pennant, did not play yesterday, the laws of Pennsylvania forbidding Sunday baseball, and meet Chicago at Shibe Park at 3:15 p.m. today. The Yankees divided a double-header at the Stadium. Brooklyn divided at Ebbets Field. The Giants won at the Polo Grounds before about 31,000. Mr. Connie Mack spent the day at home, his household states, and did not use the telephone.

columns.headline: Union Seminary chapel reopens this morning with four postcards in its porch
columns.body: The chapel of Union Theological Seminary reopens at 8 a.m. today. The four postcards received from Dr. Matthias Strand since July hang on the porch board. Two visitors looked at them on Saturday afternoon, the porter states. Neither said which chapel it was.

columns.headline: Society's recorder runs its first night at a Long Island City window
columns.body: The recorder fitted by the Phonautograph Society of Queens at the window of a Long Island City boy ran from midnight to 4 a.m. yesterday, Mr. Linus Fahey, secretary, states. The record has been taken to the Society's rooms. Six nights remain.

columns.headline: Radio Division's Mr. Pike returns to his office after 21 nights
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division returns to his office at the Customs House this morning after 21 nights at Port Washington, where WORS 1610 has not been heard since August 25, he states. Two of his men remain there through September.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 69. Monday. Mr. Mack can count now. Read on.

lead.headline: Mr. Mack finally counts to one, and the pennant comes through loud and clear
lead.deck: Shibe Park, Chicago beaten, the American League won; the park's system takes down twenty thousand people counting the last out for a manager who said he never counted
lead.body: This afternoon at Shibe Park the Athletics beat Chicago and won the American League, the first pennant in Philadelphia since 1914. For a week Mr. Connie Mack has said he had not counted, and for a week Philadelphia counted for him. At the last out the park's system took down twenty thousand people saying 'one' at once. Mr. Mack, sixty-six, shook every hand in the dugout and said, 'Now I have counted.' The Cubs are next. Our sporting man has started on Chicago.

columns.headline: Pike comes in off the wire, and his desk doesn't recognise him
columns.body: Twenty-one nights at Port Washington, and this morning Mr. Pike was back at the Customs House, shaved, with the thermos. Sixteen-ten never rang. Two of his men stay at the hut through September, and the cat Sixteen-Ten stays with them, on the camp bed Pike left.

columns.headline: The boy's window takes its first night down, and his mother takes the chair
columns.body: Midnight to four, the Society's recorder at the Long Island City window, and the mother in the kitchen chair beside it with her knitting. In the morning Mr. Fahey's man took the record away in a box. Asked what was on it, he said, 'Night.'

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'How do I ring the Athletics to say well done?'
columns.body: Sir, ask for Philadelphia, Long Distance, and say 'Shibe Park.' The operator in Philadelphia will tell you that every line to Shibe Park has been engaged since five o'clock, and that Mr. Mack is not taking calls. He is taking congratulations by post.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Philadelphia, seven o'clock: Broad Street full to the kerbs. Somebody is playing a record of the Liberty Bell. The real one does not ring.

lead.headline: Athletics win the American League pennant, beating Chicago at Shibe Park
lead.deck: First pennant for Philadelphia since 1914; Mr. Grove pitches the last three innings; Mr. Mack states that he 'has now counted'; the World Series to open in October against the National League's winner
lead.body: The Philadelphia Athletics made certain of the American League pennant at 5:02 p.m. yesterday, beating Chicago at Shibe Park by 5 to 2 before about 20,000, the club states. It is Philadelphia's first pennant since 1914. Mr. Robert Grove pitched the last three innings. Mr. Connie Mack, manager, stated that he 'has now counted.' The Chicago Cubs lead the National League by thirteen games. The park's record of the last out has been sent by wire to the Cubs' office, the Athletics' secretary states.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 372.4 on 3,820,000 shares; tone book enters 'even'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 3,820,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 372.4, a gain of 5.4. The ticker ran 12 minutes late. The tone book enters its tone at 3 p.m. as 'even,' a first this month.

columns.headline: Committee sits today on Mr. Feeney's motion for the company's load sheets
columns.body: The Committee on Public Utilities of the Board of Aldermen will sit at 2 p.m. today on Alderman John Feeney's motion that Queens Light & Power deliver its load sheets for August, the committee's clerk states. Counsel for the company will attend. Mr. Feeney's records application is heard October 9.

columns.headline: Coal wagon begins the Steinway Street round with a gelding bought at Jamaica
columns.body: The Astoria Ice Company's coal wagon began its Steinway Street round yesterday, drawn by a gelding, Duke, 9, bought at Jamaica on Friday, Mr. Gustave Pohl states. Nut coal was delivered to 41 houses. The ice truck calls on alternate days until September 30.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Harold Pike reached his office at the Customs House at 8:50 a.m., the Radio Division states, and did not leave it until 7 p.m.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 71. Tuesday. Gorman day. Six to go.

lead.headline: The calendar is printed, and Gorman finds his eleven seconds on the bill
lead.deck: Ten o'clock at the Appellate Division clerk's window: this time the clerk hands it over, and the Riverhead appeal is sixth on Monday's list
lead.body: At ten this morning Mr. Francis Gorman stepped up to the clerk's window in Brooklyn and asked, as he has asked every Tuesday since July, for the calendar of the twenty-third of September. This time the clerk handed one over, still warm from the printer. The Riverhead appeal, the eleven sealed seconds, is sixth on the list for Monday. Mr. Gorman read it twice, folded it into his hat with the date, and said 'Six days.' The people behind him applauded. The clerk bowed.

columns.headline: Coal comes to Steinway Street on four legs, and the ladies switch back on
columns.body: The coal wagon came round Steinway Street yesterday behind a gelding called Duke, nine years old, bought at Jamaica on Friday. The ladies came out to look at him. They found him satisfactory, if not Nell. Duke ate a carrot from Mrs. Pappas and has been asked back.

columns.headline: Mack takes the call he waited fifteen years for, and Chicago is on the line
columns.body: Five past five yesterday, the Athletics' pennant, and by six Mr. Mack had a telegram from the Cubs saying they would see him in October. They have not won theirs yet, but they are thirteen up. The Speaker's sporting man is already calling it the Long Distance Series.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike back at his desk, and Port Washington's line stays cold
columns.body: Mr. Pike worked eleven hours at the Customs House yesterday and did not look out of the window once, his clerk says. At Port Washington his two men sat up all night with the cat. Sixteen-ten did not ring. Sixteen-Ten, the cat, purred, which is not the same.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Brooklyn, half past ten: Mr. Gorman seen buying a new pencil. He has never needed one before.

lead.headline: Utilities committee hears the light company on Mr. Feeney's load-sheet motion
lead.deck: Company's counsel states that the sheets are 'the company's record of the company's load'; motion reported favourably by four votes to one; the Board of Aldermen to vote on Tuesday next
lead.body: The Committee on Public Utilities of the Board of Aldermen sat for 1 hour 40 minutes yesterday on Alderman John Feeney's motion that Queens Light & Power deliver its load sheets for August, the committee's clerk states. Mr. Victor Ashby, for the company, stated that the sheets are 'the company's record of the company's load' and that the company has 'nothing further to add to its page.' The committee reported the motion favourably by four votes to one. The Board of Aldermen will vote on Tuesday.

columns.headline: Mr. Gorman receives the calendar of September 23; appeal listed sixth
columns.body: The clerk of the Appellate Division states that the calendar for September 23 was printed yesterday and that Mr. Francis Gorman received the first copy at 10 a.m. His appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Riverhead record is listed sixth. He stated 'six days.'

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its twenty-sixth week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its twenty-sixth week. Senator Rufus Keel's office states that the Senator is at Saratoga.

columns.headline: Stocks ease to 371.1 on 4,010,000 shares; tone book enters 'uneven'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange eased yesterday on a volume of 4,010,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 371.1, a loss of 1.3. The ticker ran 16 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'uneven.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night at Port Washington, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 73. Wednesday. Slow day on the Street. Very slow.

lead.headline: Nobody's buying, nobody's selling, and the ticker still can't keep time
lead.deck: The quietest afternoon on the Exchange since July, three million shares and a yawn, and the tape runs fourteen minutes behind anyway; the tone book writes a word it has never used: 'slow'
lead.body: Wall Street had a quiet day today, the quietest since July, three million shares and a yawn. And the ticker ran fourteen minutes behind all the same. On a busy day nobody minds; the tape is buried. Today it had nothing to carry and carried it late. The Exchange's men opened the machine at two and found it clean. The tone book wrote 'slow,' which it has never written. The Jamaica dentist says the ticker was thinking. The Flushing undertaker says he knows the feeling.

columns.headline: Company keeps its load sheets dark, and the committee flips the switch
columns.body: Mr. Ashby for the light company told the aldermen's committee yesterday that the load sheets are 'the company's record of the company's load,' which took him forty minutes. The committee voted four to one to send Mr. Feeney's motion up. The full Board votes Tuesday.

columns.headline: Week twenty-six: the Senator goes to the races, and 'resent' stays in the stall
columns.body: Twenty-six weeks in the vault at Albany for 'resent.' Mr. Pratt has still sent nothing to the Senator, and the Senator's office says he is at Saratoga, where the racing ended in August. The office did not say what he is doing there. Listening, perhaps.

columns.headline: The dog war: the terrier goes on the register at P.S. 11 under the Danko name
columns.body: To stop the system counting him as Daniel, the teacher at P.S. 11 has entered him on the register as 'Danko, dog.' He answered the roll this morning with one bark and was marked present. Mrs. Fitch, Dr. Voight and Mrs. Ahl have all written to object to the surname.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Three o'clock, the Exchange floor: the tone book's clerk was asked to read 'slow' aloud. He read it slowly.

lead.headline: Ticker runs 14 minutes late on the lightest volume since July; cause not found
lead.deck: 3,010,000 shares traded and industrial average up 2.8 to 373.9; the Exchange's engineers open the machine at 2 p.m. and find it in order; tone book enters 'slow' for the first time
lead.body: The Stock Exchange ticker ran 14 minutes late at the close yesterday on a volume of 3,010,000 shares, the lightest since July 22, the Exchange states. The industrial average closed at 373.9, a gain of 2.8. The Exchange's engineers opened the machine at 2 p.m. and found it in order. On September 9, on 4,830,000 shares, the ticker's delay was 24 minutes. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. yesterday as 'slow,' an entry it has not made before.

columns.headline: Chicago Cubs certain of the National League pennant; Series opens October 8
columns.body: The Chicago Cubs made certain of the National League pennant yesterday, Pittsburgh losing at Boston, the league states. The World Series will open at Wrigley Field, Chicago, on October 8, the first two games to be played there and the next three at Shibe Park.

columns.headline: Referee to hear the Lindqvist record alone this morning at the courthouse
columns.body: Mr. Ezra Coombe, referee in the action of Mrs. Cora Lindqvist against Mr. Abner Toll, will hear the sealed record of her bedroom alone at 10 a.m. today in a room of the Long Island City courthouse, Justice Hiram Brett states. The machine has been tested with a blank.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society's recorder completes its fourth night at the window
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society's recorder at a Long Island City window completed its fourth night at 4 a.m. today, Mr. Linus Fahey states. Asked whether the records so far differ, Mr. Fahey stated that the Society 'compares at the end, not during.' Three nights remain.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd expedition reports by wire 41 degrees below zero at Little America and the dog teams in training; the message concerned harness.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 74. Thursday. The old judge is in the locked room.

lead.headline: Three hours behind a locked door, and the referee comes out with one word
lead.deck: Mr. Coombe, eighty-one, sits alone with the widow's bedroom from ten till twelve minutes past one, writes one word on a card, seals it, and won't say it aloud; Justice Brett opens it tomorrow
lead.body: At ten this morning Mr. Ezra Coombe went into a small room at the Long Island City courthouse with a machine, a chair, a jug of water and Mrs. Lindqvist's bedroom, and a bailiff locked the door. At twelve minutes past one he knocked. He had written one word on a card and sealed it. Asked what he heard, he said, 'What?' Asked again, he said, 'Tomorrow.' Mrs. Lindqvist sat on a bench in the corridor the whole time. She did not knit.

columns.headline: The Cubs clinch by long distance, and the Series line is booked to Chicago
columns.body: The Cubs won the National League yesterday without lifting a bat: Pittsburgh lost at Boston and that was that. So it is the Athletics and the Cubs from the eighth of October, two in Chicago, three in Philadelphia. Mr. Mack has sent his compliments. Mr. McCarthy has sent his back.

columns.headline: Byrd's dogs go into training, and Little America puts the huskies on the line
columns.body: Forty-one below at Little America, and Commander Byrd's dog drivers have the teams in harness again, getting them fit for the long haul south before the November flight. The message home was about harness. The Record's window played it twice. Several Jackson Avenue dogs barked back.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why is the ticker slow when nothing is happening?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator does not run the ticker. She notes only that yesterday, when the Exchange was quietest, her brokers' calls were longest, and that three brokers in Jamaica asked her what time it was. She told them. They did not believe her either.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Courthouse, two o'clock: Mr. Toll's counsel asked to see the envelope. He was shown the envelope.

lead.headline: Referee hears the Lindqvist record alone for 3 hours 12 minutes; report sealed
lead.deck: Mr. Ezra Coombe delivers one sealed word to the clerk at 1:12 p.m.; Justice Brett to open it at 10 a.m. today; the tenant waits in the corridor throughout; the record returned to its box
lead.body: Mr. Ezra Coombe, referee in the action of Mrs. Cora Lindqvist against her landlord, Mr. Abner Toll, heard the record of her bedroom alone yesterday from 10 a.m. until 1:12 p.m. in a locked room of the Long Island City courthouse, the clerk states. He delivered his report to the clerk in a sealed envelope. Justice Hiram Brett will open it in court at 10 a.m. today. The record was returned to its box and sealed again. Mrs. Lindqvist waited in the corridor throughout.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 375.2 on 3,900,000 shares; tone book enters 'even'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 3,900,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 375.2, a gain of 1.3. The ticker ran 10 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'even.'

columns.headline: Athletics to receive applications for Series tickets by post only
columns.body: The Athletics will receive applications for World Series tickets by post only, beginning Monday, the club states, for the three games at Shibe Park on October 11, 12 and 14. Applications by telephone will not be accepted. The operators at Philadelphia have been so informed.

columns.headline: Byrd expedition fixes a geological party's journey south for November
columns.body: Commander Richard E. Byrd's expedition states by wire that Professor Laurence M. Gould's geological party will leave Little America by dog team early in November to lay depots for the polar flight. The temperature was 41 below. The message was played in this newspaper's window.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states, at Port Washington or elsewhere.

speaker.ear: Cooler. High 68. Friday. Twenty-five Fridays. The judge opened it.

lead.headline: One word from a one-eared judge, and the widow's bedroom goes off the air
lead.deck: Justice Brett opens Mr. Coombe's envelope at ten: 'Yes.' A sleeping room under section 9, the record to be destroyed and heard by no one else; Mr. Toll's lawyer asks what else the referee heard
lead.body: At ten this morning Justice Brett slit Mr. Coombe's envelope and read the word out: 'Yes.' The record is of a sleeping room under section 9 of the Listening Act, and the Justice ordered it destroyed tomorrow, unheard by anyone but the referee. Mr. Toll's lawyer stood up and asked what else Mr. Coombe had heard in three hours. Mr. Coombe, in the front row, said 'Yes' again, which may have been an answer. Mrs. Lindqvist cried. Her lawyer's chair stayed upright this time.

columns.headline: Party Line's twenty-fifth Friday, and the parcel window is still on hold
columns.body: Twenty-five Fridays. Party Line at the window at four, the light going earlier, and at five under the board. No tin from Corona. Smith the treasurer has bought the linemen's lodge a new ball. Sergeant Moran has been asked to bowl with it. He has.

columns.headline: A London promoter's shares go dead on the line, and the cable crackles
columns.body: Mr. Clarence Hatry's companies' shares were suspended on the London Stock Exchange this morning, and the cable carried the news across before the brokers in London had finished their tea. The Street had a bad afternoon. The Jamaica dentist says London is a long way off. The undertaker says nothing is.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Port Washington's men count the days, and the cat keeps watch
columns.body: Twenty-six nights at the hut and nothing on the line. Mr. Pike's two men have ten nights left, and have started a calendar on the wall. Sixteen-Ten, the cat, has caught a mouse and left it on the receiver. The office boy says it is a message.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Toll, outside the courthouse: he will not appeal. His tenants, outside his building: they have taken down one blanket each.

lead.headline: Justice Brett orders the Lindqvist bedroom record destroyed on referee's 'yes'
lead.deck: First ruling under section 9 of the Listening Act; record to be burned at the courthouse at 11 a.m. today, heard by no person but the referee; Mr. Toll does not appeal; costs to the tenant
lead.body: Justice Hiram Brett yesterday ordered destroyed the record of Mrs. Cora Lindqvist's bedroom made by the system of her landlord, Mr. Abner Toll, the referee, Mr. Ezra Coombe, having reported in one word, 'Yes,' that it records a sleeping room under section 9 of the Listening Act. It is the first ruling under the section. The record will be burned in the courthouse boiler at 11 a.m. today. Mr. Toll stated that he will not appeal. Costs were awarded to Mrs. Lindqvist.

columns.headline: Week's count: 2,602 night calls on the tone; operators enter 'steady' nightly
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 2,602 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 2,711, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The operators' sheets enter it as 'steady' on each night. Dr. Emil Rastin's readings are 'as before.'

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twenty-fifth Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twenty-fifth Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal attended the parcel window from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Stocks fall to 368.6 after London suspensions; tone book enters 'dropped'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on 4,880,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 368.6, a loss of 6.6, after the London suspension of the Hatry companies' shares was cabled at 10:40 a.m. The ticker ran 27 minutes late. The tone book entered 'dropped.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 66. Saturday. The boiler had a busy morning.

lead.headline: The widow's nights go up the courthouse flue, and nobody gets an earful
lead.deck: Eleven o'clock in the Long Island City boiler room: Mrs. Lindqvist, two lawyers, a bailiff and a stoker watch three months of her sleep go into the fire; the referee says he was there already
lead.body: At eleven this morning, in the basement of the Long Island City courthouse, the stoker opened the boiler door and the bailiff put in the box, wax and all. Mrs. Lindqvist watched it go with her hat on. Mr. Varga and Mr. Orr watched too, from opposite sides. It burned in about a minute, with a smell of candles. Mr. Coombe was asked to attend and declined; he said he had been there already. Afterwards Mrs. Lindqvist went home to Elmhurst to sleep.

columns.headline: Twenty-six hundred calls, and the Hum keeps a steady line all week
columns.body: Two thousand six hundred and two calls about the night tone this week, a few less than last, and every night the operators wrote the same word: 'steady.' Dr. Rastin on his roof agrees. The light company is still on its one page. Nobody wrote 'nearer.'

columns.headline: The boy's window signs off tonight, and the Society keeps the wax in a box
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society's recorder at the Long Island City window does its seventh night tonight and comes out in the morning. Mr. Fahey says the Society compares at the end, not during. The boy asked to hear one. Mr. Fahey said 1978.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a Douglaston wedding puts the vows on two records
columns.body: Darlings, Miss Harriet Bloom married Mr. Thomas Ryland at Douglaston this afternoon, and both families hired a recorder, and neither would share. So the vows are on two records, and one of them has the groom's 'I will' a little late. The Listening Lady thinks it was the other one.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Elmhurst, nine o'clock: Mrs. Lindqvist's bedroom light is out. Mr. Toll's system has been switched off at the board, his counsel says, 'for the present.'

editorial.headline: Silence was golden; she was not
editorial.body: We are told by our women readers, in letters that grow longer every week, that the Speaker is unfair to Lilith. We answer them. In ten months the woman has embarrassed an alderman, a doctor, an assemblyman, a store manager, a commissioner, a school board, a judge twice, an inspector, a fire inspector, a realty company, a beach censor, an ice trust and a candidate for borough president, and has paid widows, nurses, teachers, shopgirls, laundresses, operators and children's shoes. Laid end to end, this is not a record of good deeds. It is a pattern. And a pattern, readers, is exactly what a villain has. We rest our case. Miss Penrose has typed it twice.

record.ear: Fair. High 67. Low 49. Autumn begins tomorrow.

lead.headline: Lindqvist bedroom record burned in the courthouse boiler at 11:04 a.m.
lead.deck: Tenant, both counsel and a court officer present; referee declines to attend; Mr. Toll's system switched off at its board, his counsel states; Senate committee at Albany asks for the order
lead.body: The record of Mrs. Cora Lindqvist's bedroom was burned in the boiler of the Long Island City courthouse at 11:04 a.m. yesterday under the order of Justice Hiram Brett, the clerk states. Mrs. Lindqvist, Mr. Lucius Varga, Mr. Raymond Orr and a court officer were present. Mr. Ezra Coombe, the referee, declined to attend. Mr. Orr stated that Mr. Toll's system had been switched off at its board. The Senate committee that drafted the Listening Act has asked for a copy of the order.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society removes its recorder from the Long Island City window
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society's recorder was removed from a Long Island City window at 4:30 a.m. today after seven nights, Mr. Linus Fahey states. The seven records will be compared with the two the Society retains from the boy's own recorder. No date for the comparison has been fixed.

columns.headline: Appellate Division sits tomorrow; the Riverhead appeal listed sixth
columns.body: The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court, Second Department, sits at 10 a.m. tomorrow in Brooklyn after the summer recess, the clerk states. Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Board of Elections' Riverhead record is listed sixth.

columns.headline: Ice companies' last daily rounds on September 30; nut coal up 25 cents
columns.body: The autumnal equinox falls tomorrow, the Weather Bureau states. The Queens ice companies make their last daily rounds on September 30, after which ice will be delivered on order only. Nut coal stands at 14 dollars 25 a ton, a rise of 25 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Stocks closed the week yesterday at 366.0 on 2,060,000 shares at a short session, a loss of 2.6; the tone book entered 'low.'

speaker.ear: Fair. High 67. Sunday. Last day of summer. Coat on the hook, not in the cupboard.

lead.headline: Summer hangs up tomorrow, and Queens switches over to the coal man's frequency
lead.deck: Equinox Monday; the ice men's last daily round next Monday; nut coal up a quarter; the maples on Northern Boulevard turning, and the Flushing Meadow smelling of leaves for once
lead.body: Summer ends tomorrow, the Weather Bureau says, and Queens is ready. The ice men make their last daily round next Monday, and after that you will have to ask. Nut coal has gone up a quarter, which the coal men call the season. The maples on Northern Boulevard have turned at the top. Every porch in Kew Gardens has been swept twice. A parlour set in Woodside played the Saturday dance band with the window open, and nobody complained, because it was a good band.

columns.headline: The boy's window goes quiet, and Mr. Fahey goes home with seven records
columns.body: Half past four this morning, the Society's man unscrewed the recorder from the Long Island City window and took it away with seven records under his arm. The boy's mother made him tea. The boy slept through it. He has the night, he says. They only have the records.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will Gorman win tomorrow?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator does not know. She knows that Mr. Gorman has asked her twice this week for the correct time, to the second, and that she gave it him, and that he thanked her. That is more than the Board of Elections has done for him in ten months.

columns.headline: The dog war: the register keeps the terrier, and the owners keep writing
columns.body: The terrier has been marked present at P.S. 11 four days running as 'Danko, dog.' Mrs. Fitch has written to the Board of Education, Dr. Voight to the Superintendent, Mrs. Ahl to the teacher. The teacher has written back to all three: 'He is very punctual.'

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Brooklyn, six o'clock: Mr. Gorman seen outside the Appellate Division, timing the walk from the tram. Four minutes. He will leave five.

lead.headline: Yankees win twice at the Stadium; Athletics rest their pitchers and lose
lead.deck: Mr. Ruth hits a home run in each game before about 40,000; Brooklyn wins at Ebbets Field; Giants lose at Pittsburgh; Athletics, Mr. Grove and Mr. Earnshaw rested for October, lose at Washington
lead.body: The Yankees won both games of a double-header from Detroit at the Stadium yesterday before about 40,000, Mr. Babe Ruth hitting a home run in each. The Athletics, resting Mr. Robert Grove and Mr. George Earnshaw for the World Series, lost at Washington. Brooklyn won at Ebbets Field. The Giants lost at Pittsburgh. The Cubs won at Cincinnati. The Athletics' office states that the post office at Philadelphia held 11,000 applications for Series tickets on Saturday, two days before the club opens them.

columns.headline: Appellate Division returns from recess today with 61 appeals undecided
columns.body: The Appellate Division returns from its summer recess at 10 a.m. today with 61 appeals undecided, among them Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Riverhead record, listed sixth, the clerk states. Decisions in reserved appeals are customarily handed down at the first sitting.

columns.headline: Terrier entered on a P.S. 11 register 'for the purposes of the system only'
columns.body: The principal of P.S. 11, Sunnyside, states that a wire-haired terrier has been entered on a classroom register as 'Danko, dog,' 'for the purposes of the system only,' the system having entered his bark as a pupil's answer. District Superintendent Lyle Ambler has asked for a report.

columns.headline: Valves at 18 cents in Queens, a rise of one cent; eggs at 52 cents
columns.body: Receiving valves sold at 18 cents in Queens on Saturday, a rise of 1 cent on the week, eggs at 52 cents a dozen, unchanged, and nut coal at 14 dollars 25 a ton, the Department of Markets states. Valve dealers report sales 'for the market news.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 70. Monday. Autumn. And Gorman's day. Hats off.

lead.headline: Ten months on hold, and the court finally puts Gorman's eleven seconds through
lead.deck: The Appellate Division reverses Justice Rourke three to two: the Board must play its sealed seconds to counsel in chambers; Chairman Delaney heads for Albany; Mr. Gorman says nothing at all
lead.body: At twenty past ten this morning, sixth on the list, the Appellate Division ruled on the eleven sealed seconds of the Riverhead record, and Mr. Gorman won. Three judges to two: the Board of Elections must play the seconds to counsel in Justice Rourke's chambers, on a day to be fixed. Chairman Delaney says he will ask leave to go to the Court of Appeals. Mr. Gorman stood, put on his hat with the date in it, and walked out without a word. Thirty-seven sittings. He had said enough.

columns.headline: The A's rest the big arms in Washington, and lose with the volume down
columns.body: Mr. Mack played at Washington yesterday with Grove and Earnshaw in the stands, and lost. Nobody in Philadelphia minded. Eleven thousand of them have already posted for Series tickets, two days before the club would open them. The postmen are not amused.

columns.headline: The dog war: 'Danko, dog' gets an inspector, and the inspector gets a bark
columns.body: Superintendent Ambler has asked P.S. 11 for a report on its terrier pupil. The principal sent half a page, ending: 'Attendance perfect.' Mr. Ambler sent an inspector. The terrier was present at nine this morning. The inspector came at ten. The terrier had gone home at half past nine.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? A week to go at Port Washington, and the cat's in charge
columns.body: One more week for Mr. Pike's two men at the Port Washington hut, then home. The cat Sixteen-Ten has taken the camp bed. Sixteen-ten the station has taken nothing. The harbour master says he will keep the cat when they go. He is not sure he will keep the hut.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Board of Elections, four o'clock: Chairman Delaney declines to say what is on the eleven seconds. Commissioner Wallach says he will be in chambers 'with a pencil.'

lead.headline: Appellate Division orders the Riverhead record's 11 seconds played to counsel
lead.deck: Justice Rourke reversed by three votes to two; the seconds to be played in his chambers on a day he fixes; the Board of Elections to seek leave to appeal to the Court of Appeals
lead.body: The Appellate Division, Second Department, yesterday reversed by three votes to two the order of Justice Thaddeus Rourke sealing 11 seconds of the Board of Elections' record of the Riverhead transmission of January 3, and directed that they be played to counsel in his chambers on a day he will fix. Justice Albert Sayre wrote for the court that a sealed count 'does not seal the wire.' Chairman Delaney stated that the Board will seek leave to appeal. Mr. Francis Gorman made no statement.

columns.headline: Board of Aldermen votes this afternoon on Mr. Feeney's load-sheet motion
columns.body: The Board of Aldermen will vote at 1:30 p.m. today on Alderman John Feeney's motion, reported favourably by the Committee on Public Utilities, that Queens Light & Power deliver its load sheets for August. Mr. Feeney's records application is heard on October 9.

columns.headline: Stocks fall to 362.1 on 4,320,000 shares; tone book enters 'low'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 4,320,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 362.1, a loss of 3.9. The ticker ran 20 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'low' again.

columns.headline: Nine Queens schools to take the roll by system from today
columns.body: The classroom systems of the nine Queens schools that took the roll by hand in the first fortnight are ready, the Board of Education states, and take it from today, twice, under District Superintendent Lyle Ambler's order. The discrepancy across Queens stood at 31 answers on Friday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 64. Tuesday. The aldermen voted. The company wrote back fast.

lead.headline: Aldermen ask for the load sheets, and the light company sends one more page
lead.deck: Forty-one to nineteen for Mr. Feeney's motion at half past two; at a quarter to four a messenger brings the company's answer, one page again, and Mr. Feeney reads it aloud again
lead.body: The Board of Aldermen voted forty-one to nineteen this afternoon to ask Queens Light & Power for its load sheets for August. It took eleven minutes. At a quarter to four a messenger in a company cap came into the chamber with an envelope. Inside was one page, like the last one. Mr. Feeney read it aloud: the sheets are 'the company's record of the company's load and are not for publication.' Twenty-two seconds, his watch says. He will ask again on October 9, in court.

columns.headline: Gorman wins, and the Board tries to dial Albany, which can't be done
columns.body: Chairman Delaney says the Board will ask leave to take the eleven seconds to the Court of Appeals. Until then they stay sealed. Mr. Gorman, asked how he felt, said the appeal was 'expected' and went to buy sandwiches. Mr. Wallach has a pencil.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why is my coal man ringing before the ice man?'
columns.body: Madam, because it is the end of September. The ice man has one more week of daily rounds; the coal man has all winter. The operator says that this morning she put through more calls for coal than for ice for the first time since April. She has noted it.

columns.headline: The Street goes on the low setting for a second day, and the brokers pipe down
columns.body: Stocks down again yesterday, near four points, and the tone book wrote 'low' for the second day running. In the Jamaica brokers' offices nobody whistled. The dentist has bought more. The undertaker has bought a coat. He says it is the season.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Four o'clock: the light company's messenger, asked his name, said he was 'the company.' He was about nineteen.

lead.headline: Board of Aldermen asks the light company for its load sheets by 41 votes to 19
lead.deck: Mr. Feeney's motion carried in 11 minutes; company's reply delivered by hand at 3:45 p.m. states that the sheets 'are not for publication'; records application stands for October 9
lead.body: The Board of Aldermen yesterday adopted by 41 votes to 19 Alderman John Feeney's motion that Queens Light & Power deliver to the Board its load sheets for August, the City Clerk states. At 3:45 p.m. a messenger delivered the company's reply, of one page, which states that the sheets 'are the company's record of the company's load and are not for publication.' Mr. Feeney read the reply to the Board. His application for the records will be heard in the Supreme Court on October 9.

columns.headline: Ohio has no trust of the name on file, Mr. Crane states; Ditmars seal remains
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane's office states that the Ohio Secretary of State has no Ditmars Holding Trust on file. Mr. Royal Haskin of Cleveland replied by wire that the trust 'is not of Ohio.' He did not say of where. The seal on the Ditmars Avenue room remains.

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its twenty-seventh week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its twenty-seventh week. Senator Rufus Keel has telegraphed from Saratoga, of one word: 'Still.'

columns.headline: Stocks fall to 355.4 on 4,560,000 shares; tone book enters 'dropped'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 4,560,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 355.4, a loss of 6.7. The ticker ran 26 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'dropped.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night at Port Washington, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 66. Wednesday. Ohio says, not us. Keel says, still.

lead.headline: Ohio has never heard of the Ditmars trust, and its lawyer goes out of range
lead.deck: Mr. Crane writes to Columbus and gets 'no such trust'; Mr. Haskin wires back that the trust 'is not of Ohio'; of where, he does not say; the sealed room on Ditmars Avenue keeps its own counsel
lead.body: Mr. Crane, still holding the seal on the Ditmars Avenue room that heard the fire first, wrote to the Secretary of State at Columbus about the Ditmars Holding Trust of Cleveland. Columbus wrote back: no such trust on file. Mr. Crane wired Mr. Haskin. Mr. Haskin wired back that the trust 'is not of Ohio.' Mr. Crane wired: 'Of where?' That was Monday. Cleveland has not answered. Four directories have the house, and nobody in it.

columns.headline: Week twenty-seven: the Senator wires one word, and it isn't 'resent'
columns.body: Twenty-seven weeks in the vault at Albany. This time the Senator wired before he was asked, from Saratoga, one word: 'Still.' Mr. Pratt has filed it with 'Well. Listening.' Read together they make a sentence. The Speaker would rather not say which.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Jackson Heights dances with the house system turned down
columns.body: Darlings, the Jackson Heights Garden Club opened its autumn dances on Saturday, and the band was hired, and the house system was turned low, at the club's request, to save the members' blushes. The Listening Lady's blushes were saved also. She was standing by the punch.

columns.headline: Valves go up a cent, and the Street's bad news costs more to hear
columns.body: Valves were eighteen cents in Queens on Saturday, up a penny, the Department of Markets says, because everybody wants to hear the market go down sooner. Eggs held at fifty-two. The valve men say it is the season. Everybody says it is the season.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Cleveland, five o'clock: Mr. Haskin's office says Mr. Haskin is travelling. It did not say where. It said 'the trust does not.'

lead.headline: Exchange line to Maspeth answered with the call sign WORS 1610 at 2:14 a.m.
lead.deck: Queens Exchange Position 12 rings a Maspeth subscriber for a Woodside caller; the line answers with the call sign and four seconds of tone; the subscriber's bell did not ring, he states; Radio Division takes the position's record
lead.body: At 2:14 a.m. yesterday the operator at Position 12 of the Queens Exchange rang a Maspeth subscriber's line for a caller in Woodside, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The line was answered with 'W, O, R, S, sixteen-ten,' about four seconds of tone, and cleared. The subscriber, Mr. Anton Ruzicka, states that his bell did not ring and that he was asleep. The position's record was given to Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division at 9 a.m. The operator completed her shift.

columns.headline: Stocks fall to 352.0 on 4,720,000 shares; tone book enters 'low, thin'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 4,720,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 352.0, a loss of 3.4. The ticker ran 24 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'low, thin.'

columns.headline: Company's box at the General Post Office emptied on Saturday by a keyholder
columns.body: The Post Office states that the box at the General Post Office given as the address of Signal Ground Rents Inc. was emptied on Saturday by a person holding its key. Mr. Nathan Ewald's two letters were among its contents. They have not been answered. The October rent is due Tuesday.

columns.headline: Athletics receive 63,000 applications for Series tickets in three days
columns.body: The Athletics state that 63,000 applications for World Series tickets were received by post in the first three days, for about 33,000 seats at each of the three games at Shibe Park. Allotment will be made by drawing. Telephone applications continue to be refused.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Harold Pike states that he has heard the record of Position 12 'several times' and has no statement.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 63. Thursday. Sixteen-ten picked up. Read it twice.

lead.headline: Sixteen-ten picks up a Maspeth line at two in the morning, and nobody rang it
lead.deck: Position 12 rings for Woodside and gets the call sign and four seconds of tone; the Maspeth man was asleep and his bell never went; Mr. Pike has the record and nothing to say about it
lead.body: Two fourteen yesterday morning, a quiet night at the Queens Exchange. A Woodside caller asked for a Maspeth number, and the girl at Position 12 rang it. Somebody picked up. A voice said 'W, O, R, S, sixteen-ten,' then came four seconds of tone, and the line cleared. The Maspeth baker, Mr. Ruzicka, says his bell never rang and he was asleep. Mr. Pike has the record. He has heard it several times, and not said of what.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who was the Woodside caller?'
columns.body: Sir, the operator cannot say; the Exchange keeps its callers' names. She can say that the Woodside caller rang again at 2:20 and asked for the same number, and was put through, and got Mr. Ruzicka, who was very cross. That is all. It was enough.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike rings at Maspeth, and the office boy reaches for a pin
columns.body: Mr. Pike was at the Maspeth baker's at noon looking at a telephone on a wall. He did not lift it. He went to the Exchange and sat at Position 12 for an hour. The office boy has put a red pin in Maspeth, his fifth. He has run out of red.

columns.headline: Somebody opens the company's box, and Ewald's letters go off the shelf
columns.body: Somebody with a key emptied Signal Ground Rents' box at the General Post Office on Saturday, the Post Office says, and took Mr. Ewald's two letters with everything else. No answer yet. October's rent is due Tuesday. Mr. Ewald says the company can now read. Whether it can write is another thing.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Position 12's operator, who would not give her name, went back on shift at midnight. She asked to be moved. The supervisor moved her to Position 11.

lead.headline: Bank of England raises its rate to 6 1/2 per cent; Exchange recovers by 3.1
lead.deck: Rate change carried by cable at 7:10 a.m.; industrial average closes at 355.1 on 4,040,000 shares after a lower opening; tone book enters 'uneven'; brokers' loans at a record
lead.body: The Bank of England raised its discount rate from 5 1/2 to 6 1/2 per cent yesterday, the London cable states, the change being carried to New York at 7:10 a.m. Prices on the Stock Exchange opened lower and recovered in the afternoon, the industrial average closing at 355.1, a gain of 3.1, on 4,040,000 shares. The ticker ran 18 minutes late. The tone book enters its tone at 3 p.m. as 'uneven.'

columns.headline: Radio Division examines the Maspeth line; no fault found, Mr. Pike states
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division examined the Maspeth subscriber's line and instrument yesterday with two linemen of the New York Telephone Company, and found no fault, he states. The record of Position 12 is retained by the Division. WORS 1610 was not heard elsewhere that night.

columns.headline: Mr. Ewald to deposit the Arcade's October rent with the clerk on Tuesday
columns.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald states that he will deposit the Vantry Arcade's October rent, 412 dollars, with the Municipal Court clerk at 10 a.m. on Tuesday, after which the clerk will hold 2,060 dollars for Signal Ground Rents Inc. Mr. Ewald states that he will not write a third letter.

columns.headline: Byrd's monoplane run for one hour on skis at 38 degrees below zero
columns.body: Commander Richard E. Byrd's expedition states by wire that the Ford monoplane Floyd Bennett, fitted with skis, was run for one hour at Little America yesterday at 38 degrees below zero. The message, concerning grease, was played in this newspaper's window, the engines after it.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 62. Friday. Twenty-six Fridays. Mind the horse.

lead.headline: A coal horse climbs the El at Corona and puts the Flushing line on hold
lead.deck: Twenty to eight, the Corona platform: one wagon horse, nineteen minutes, and four thousand riders late for work and delighted about it; the horse is led down backwards
lead.body: At twenty to eight this morning a coal-wagon horse named Bess, left at the kerb on Roosevelt Avenue while her driver carried a sack, walked up the stairs of the Corona station and stood on the platform looking toward Manhattan. The Flushing trains stopped for nineteen minutes. Four thousand people were late for work, and not one complained, because they had all seen a horse on the El. Her driver and a patrolman led her down backwards. She was given an apple. He was given a summons.

columns.headline: Party Line's twenty-sixth Friday, and Position 43 hears nothing from Corona
columns.body: Twenty-six Fridays. Party Line at the window at four, then a walk along the board to Position 12, which she has not done before. At five, under the board. No tin from Corona. The supervisor has noted the walk. She has not noted why.

columns.headline: London ups the rate a whole point, and the cable rings Wall Street at breakfast
columns.body: The Bank of England put its rate up to six and a half yesterday, a full point, and the cable had it in New York by ten past seven. The Street opened low and came back by three. The Jamaica dentist says London cannot frighten him. The undertaker's coat has arrived.

columns.headline: Pike gives the Maspeth line a clean bill, and the baker leaves it off the hook
columns.body: Mr. Pike and two telephone linemen spent yesterday with the Maspeth baker's telephone and found nothing wrong with it. The baker watched them, floury. When they had gone he took the earpiece off its hook and left it off. He says he will put it back when somebody explains.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Corona, six o'clock: Bess the coal horse is back in harness and has been turned to face away from the station.

lead.headline: Week's count: 2,588 night calls on the tone, 'steady' on all seven nights
lead.deck: Second week without a change in the operators' entry; Brooklyn door at 1,402; Dr. Rastin's Corona readings 'as before'; the Maspeth call entered separately at the Radio Division's request
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 2,588 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 2,602, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The operators' sheets enter the tone as 'steady' on each of the seven nights, the second week without a change of word. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his Corona readings are 'as before.' The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 1,402. The call of Wednesday morning to Maspeth has been entered separately at the Radio Division's request.

columns.headline: Coal-wagon horse on the elevated platform at Corona holds Flushing trains
columns.body: Trains of the Flushing line were held for 19 minutes at 7:40 a.m. yesterday when a coal-wagon horse climbed the stairs of the Corona station of the elevated and stood on the platform, the Transit Commission states. Its driver was summoned for leaving it untied. The horse was unhurt.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twenty-sixth Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twenty-sixth Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal attended the parcel window from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m., and Position 12 at 4:40 p.m.

columns.headline: Fifth postcard from Dr. Strand shows the chapel door open; no message
columns.body: Union Seminary states that it received a fifth postcard from Dr. Matthias Strand yesterday, posted at Bangor on September 16. It shows the door of the same chapel, open, the interior not visible. The reverse bears the address and nothing else. It has been pinned in the chapel porch.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Stocks fell yesterday to 344.6 on 4,830,000 shares, a loss of 10.5; the tone book entered 'dropped.'

speaker.ear: Fair. High 64. Saturday. Strand's door is open. We're not going in.

lead.headline: Strand's fifth card arrives, and this time the chapel door is off the hook
lead.deck: Bangor postmark, nothing on the back but the seminary's address; the same Welsh chapel, the same door, open now, and inside nothing a camera could manage; up it goes on the porch board
lead.body: Five postcards since July from Dr. Matthias Strand, each of the same Welsh chapel and each a little nearer, the fourth at the door, shut. Yesterday's, posted at Bangor on the sixteenth, shows the door open. Inside it is dark; a photograph is dear and cannot see far into a chapel. The back carries the seminary's address and nothing else. The porter has pinned it in the porch with the other four. He says some of the students now use the side door.

columns.headline: Twenty-five hundred calls and one word all week: the Hum holds the line
columns.body: Two thousand five hundred and eighty-eight calls about the night tone this week, and seven nights of 'steady' on the operators' sheets. Dr. Rastin says 'as before.' Brooklyn's door says fourteen hundred and two. The Hum, it seems, has settled in for the autumn. So have we.

columns.headline: Ten points off on Friday, and the Street's tone book runs out of new words
columns.body: Down ten and a half yesterday, the worst day since the Babson fright, and the tone book wrote 'dropped' for the fourth time this month. The clerk says he has the words he needs. The Jamaica dentist has stopped buying. He says he is listening.

columns.headline: The dog war: 'Danko, dog' passes inspection, and the owners miss the bell
columns.body: Superintendent Ambler's inspector came to P.S. 11 at nine on Thursday this time and found the terrier present and quiet under the radiator. The report says 'no objection.' All three owners came at noon to claim him, together. He had gone home. Nobody knows whose.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Union Seminary, five o'clock: the porter reports the porch board visited by thirty-one people since noon, and the side door by most of the faculty.

editorial.headline: First cold night; the Speaker remembers November
editorial.body: The first cold night came on Thursday and the Speaker's editor, reaching for his overcoat, found in its pocket a single black silk stocking tied in a spider's knot, and a card: It was cold last November, too. You called me a menace that week. I hope you are warm. This paper does not frighten easily. This paper has, however, changed its locks, its tailor and its overcoat. We have asked Miss Penrose whether she saw anybody enter our office. She says she saw nobody she did not expect. We have asked her what she means by that. She says she means what she says, which is more, she adds, than most of the men she types for.

lead.headline: Queens congregations prepare for the holy days; systems to be switched off
lead.deck: Rosh Hashanah begins at sundown on Friday, October 4, and Yom Kippur at sundown on October 13; fourteen of the borough's 22 synagogues to switch off their systems for the services
lead.body: The Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah, begins at sundown on Friday, October 4, and the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, at sundown on Sunday, October 13, the Queens Board of Rabbis states. Fourteen of the borough's 22 synagogues will switch off their house systems for the services of both holy days, at the request of their rabbis. The shofar will be sounded in person only. Rabbi Isaac Lerner of Congregation Beth Israel, Woodside, stated that 'what is said on those days is not said to a record.'

columns.headline: Ice companies make their last daily rounds tomorrow; delivery on order after
columns.body: The Queens ice companies make their last daily rounds of the season tomorrow, the Ice Dealers' Association states, after which ice will be delivered on order by telephone only. The Astoria Ice Company's motor truck will be laid up until May. Its horses go to the coal wagons.

columns.headline: Arcade's October rent falls due on Tuesday; no reply to Mr. Ewald
columns.body: The October rent of the Vantry Arcade's eleven shops falls due on Tuesday, Mr. Nathan Ewald states. Neither of his letters to Signal Ground Rents Inc. has been answered since the company's box was emptied on September 21. The tenants will deposit with the Municipal Court clerk.

columns.headline: Radio Division's men to leave Port Washington tomorrow; hut to be closed
columns.body: The Radio Division's two men at Port Washington will leave tomorrow after 36 nights, Mr. Harold Pike states, WORS 1610 not having been heard there since August 25. The hut will be returned to the harbour master. A cat will remain with him.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Stocks closed the week yesterday at 347.2 on 2,460,000 shares at a short session, a gain of 2.6; the tone book entered 'held.'

speaker.ear: Cool. High 61. Sunday. Last day of daily ice. Wave to the truck.

lead.headline: The ice man rings his last daily bell, and Steinway Street hangs up the dish
lead.deck: Tomorrow the motor truck makes the final round of the season with Nell's bell on the horn; after that it's ice by telephone; at Jamaica, Nell has been told nothing and is eating
lead.body: Tomorrow the ice comes round for the last time this year, and then it is coal till May. The Astoria Ice Company's truck will play Nell's bell on its horn at every stop on Steinway Street, the record a lady took every Thursday for nine years. After that the truck goes into the shed, and October's ice is by telephone. Mr. Pohl says some of the ladies have asked whether the bell can be played once more at Christmas. He is thinking about it.

columns.headline: Fourteen synagogues will keep the holy days off the record
columns.body: Rosh Hashanah begins Friday at sundown and Yom Kippur the Sunday after, and fourteen of Queens' twenty-two synagogues will switch their house systems off for both. Rabbi Lerner of Woodside says what is said on those days is not said to a record. The Speaker, for once, has nothing to add.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike's men pack the thermos, and the cat stays tuned in
columns.body: Tomorrow Mr. Pike's two men leave the Port Washington hut after thirty-six nights and nothing. The harbour master keeps the hut and the cat, Sixteen-Ten, who has not been asked. The office boy says his Maspeth pin counts double.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I ring the ice man in October?'
columns.body: Madam, you can, and from Tuesday you must. Ask for the Astoria Ice Company and say how many pounds. The operator warns that the ice man will answer slower than he used to come round. He has not yet learned the telephone. Neither has his horse.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Far Rockaway, four o'clock: a shofar being practised on a back porch, heard along Beach 9th Street. Nobody recorded it. Several people listened.

lead.headline: Radio Division withdraws its men from Port Washington after 36 nights
lead.deck: WORS 1610 not heard there since August 25; Mr. Pike states that the Division's watch on the Maspeth line continues; the hut returned to the harbour master with its contents
lead.body: The Radio Division withdraws its two men from Port Washington this morning after 36 nights in a hut lent by the harbour master, Mr. Harold Pike states. WORS 1610 has not been heard there since August 25, when the Division's men took down four minutes of it. The hut will be returned to the harbour master, Mr. Silas Brewer, with its contents, among them a cat. The Division's watch on the Maspeth subscriber's line continues. Mr. Pike would not state for how long.

columns.headline: Athletics and Cubs rest their pitchers; World Series opens in eight days
columns.body: The Athletics and the Cubs rested their leading pitchers in their week-end games, the Athletics winning at Washington on Saturday and the Cubs losing at Pittsburgh yesterday. The Yankees won at the Stadium. The World Series opens at Wrigley Field, Chicago, on October 8.

columns.headline: Arcade's October rent due tomorrow; clerk to hold 2,060 dollars
columns.body: The Vantry Arcade's October rent falls due tomorrow, and Mr. Nathan Ewald will deposit it, 412 dollars, with the Municipal Court clerk at 10 a.m., the clerk then holding 2,060 dollars for Signal Ground Rents Inc. Neither of Mr. Ewald's letters has been answered.

columns.headline: Ice companies make their last daily rounds today; 312 wagons to be laid up
columns.body: The Queens ice companies make their last daily rounds of the season today, the Ice Dealers' Association states, after which 312 wagons and trucks will be laid up. Ice will be delivered on order only. The Astoria Ice Company's truck plays its bell for the last time at noon.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night at Port Washington, the Radio Division states, on the Division's last night there.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 63. Monday. Last of September. Last of the ice. Last of the hut.

lead.headline: Pike's men ring off at Port Washington, and the cat stays on the line
lead.deck: Thirty-six nights in a hut, four minutes heard in August and not a whisper since; the two Radio Division men pack their receiver and their thermos, and Sixteen-Ten declines to get in the motor
lead.body: At nine this morning Mr. Pike's two men carried their receiver out of the Port Washington hut, then the camp bed, then the second thermos, and loaded the Division's motor. Thirty-six nights; four minutes of sixteen-ten in August and nothing after. The cat they named Sixteen-Ten watched from the window. When they opened the motor door she went under the hut. The harbour master, Mr. Brewer, says she can stay. He has put his own old receiver on the shelf, he says, for the cat.

columns.headline: Eight days to the Series, and Philadelphia's postmen carry the whole line
columns.body: Eight days to the World Series and the Athletics have had seventy thousand applications by post for ninety-nine thousand seats over three games, which sounds like enough until you hear Philadelphia. The Cubs say Chicago is calmer. Our sporting man, who has rung Chicago, says it is not.

columns.headline: October goes into court tomorrow, and the clerk's pile rings up two thousand
columns.body: Tomorrow Mr. Ewald pays the Arcade's four hundred and twelve into court again, and the clerk will be minding two thousand and sixty dollars for a company that empties its box and answers nothing. His second letter is still unanswered, which is not the same as unread.

columns.headline: The ice man's last bell rings out on Steinway Street, and the dishes come in
columns.body: Noon today, the last daily round: the motor truck stopped at every door on Steinway Street and played Nell's bell from the horn one last time. Some of the ladies came out with dishes. Some came out without, just to hear it. Nell, at Jamaica, was eating.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Port Washington, six o'clock: the harbour master reports the cat in the hut, on the shelf, beside the receiver. The receiver is not switched on. He says he will not switch it on.
